questions.stem: "Wait for me at the gate," called Nadia, "and dont wander off towards the woods."
questions.explanation: The contraction of 'do not' needs an apostrophe: it should be "don't". The missing apostrophe sits inside segment C.

questions.stem: The rehearsal ran late: the lights kept failing, so the director sent everyone home at last.
questions.explanation: The colon joins two complete, balanced clauses, so a semicolon is the correct mark here, not a colon. Segment A wrongly ends with a colon.

questions.stem: Have you ever wondered why the oldest bridge in the town has never once been repaired or replaced?

segments.label: B
segments.text: why the oldest bridge in the town

questions.explanation: This is a genuine question and correctly ends with a question mark, so there is no mistake anywhere in the sentence.

questions.stem: The judges praised both girls costumes even though the second had been sewn overnight.
questions.explanation: Two girls own the costumes, so the plural possessive needs an apostrophe after the s: "girls'". The error is in segment B.

questions.stem: My grandfather (who had sailed halfway round the world before he was twenty still keeps a battered compass.
questions.explanation: A bracket opened after 'grandfather' is never closed. The closing bracket belongs before 'still' in segment D, so that segment is faulty.

questions.stem: Next tuesday the whole class will travel to the coast to study the rock pools below the cliffs.

segments.label: B
segments.text: class will travel to the coast

questions.explanation: 'Tuesday' is a day of the week and must begin with a capital letter. The lower-case 't' in segment A is the mistake.

questions.stem: The tide rose so fast that morning that before we noticed it we were cut off from the shore.

segments.label: C
segments.text: that before we noticed it we

segments.label: D
segments.text: were cut off from the shore.

questions.explanation: The introductory clause 'that before we noticed it' should be closed with a comma. Segment C is missing the comma after 'it', running the clause straight into 'we'.

questions.stem: The inspector lowered his voice. "Nobody, he murmured, is to touch a single thing in this room."
questions.explanation: The speech is interrupted, so quotation marks must close before 'he murmured'. Segment B is missing the closing quotation mark after 'Nobody,'.

questions.stem: We booked a table for the party at the new restaurant, a well known spot beside the harbour.

segments.label: B
segments.text: for the party at the new

questions.explanation: 'Well known' is a compound adjective before the noun 'spot' and needs a hyphen: 'well-known'. The error sits in segment D.

questions.stem: The path split in two, one branch climbed steeply while the other wound gently down to the lake.
questions.explanation: Two complete clauses joined here need a semicolon, not a comma; segment A should end with a semicolon after 'two'.

questions.stem: What an astonishing sight the frozen waterfall made as it glittered in the thin winter sunshine!
questions.explanation: This is an exclamation and correctly ends with an exclamation mark, so nothing in the sentence is wrong.

questions.stem: She promised the letter would arrive by Friday, but its now Sunday and nothing has come.
questions.explanation: Here 'it's' means 'it is' and needs an apostrophe. 'Its' without one is the possessive, which is wrong in segment C.

questions.stem: For the long hike we packed water dried fruit, a map and a small first-aid kit in the old rucksack.

segments.label: A
segments.text: For the long hike we packed

questions.explanation: The list needs a comma after the first item 'water'. Segment B is missing that comma between 'water' and 'dried fruit'.

questions.stem: The oldest map — drawn long before the railway arrived and hopelessly out of date was pinned above the desk.
questions.explanation: A pair of dashes marks the parenthesis, but only the opening dash appears. The closing dash is missing before 'was' in segment D.

questions.stem: The river thames winds through the heart of the city before it finally reaches the open sea.

segments.label: B
segments.text: through the heart of the city

questions.explanation: 'Thames' is the name of a particular river and must be capitalised. The lower-case 't' in segment A is the error.

questions.stem: The captain turned to us and said, The storm will pass before midnight."
questions.explanation: The opening quotation mark is missing before the spoken words. Segment C should begin with a quotation mark before 'The storm'.

questions.stem: She had one ambition above all others; to sail single-handed right around the world.
questions.explanation: What follows explains the single ambition just announced, so a colon is needed, not a semicolon. Segment B wrongly uses a semicolon where a colon belongs.

questions.stem: The gardener showed us how to prune the roses so that next summer the bush's would bloom again.
questions.explanation: 'Bushes' is a plain plural, not a possessive, so it takes no apostrophe. The apostrophe in segment D is the mistake.

questions.stem: The tired old dog by the fire, snored loudly through the whole of the afternoon.
questions.explanation: A single comma should never separate a subject from its verb. Segment B wrongly places a comma between 'fire' and the verb 'snored'.

questions.stem: On the last day of term we read a chapter from oliver Twist and discussed the ending.

segments.label: A
segments.text: On the last day of term

questions.explanation: 'Oliver' is a name and must start with a capital letter. The lower-case 'o' in segment C is the error.

questions.stem: "Leave the window open," she whispered, "so we can hear the nightingale sing."
questions.explanation: The speech is correctly punctuated: the quotation marks open and close properly and the comma sits inside the first set, so there is no mistake.

questions.stem: The museum has just opened a twenty first century wing full of glowing screens and moving models.
questions.explanation: 'Twenty-first' is a compound number used before a noun and needs a hyphen. Segment B is missing the hyphen in 'twenty first'.

questions.stem: Only one player was missing from the whole squad that afternoon, and everyone guessed the reason; injury.
questions.explanation: The single word naming the reason is announced by 'the reason', so a colon should introduce it, not a semicolon. Segment D wrongly uses a semicolon before 'injury'.

questions.stem: The childrens laughter echoed across the empty hall long after the last of them had gone home.

segments.label: C
segments.text: long after the last of them

questions.explanation: 'Children' is already plural, so the possessive is 'children's'. The missing apostrophe in segment A is the mistake.

questions.stem: The old lighthouse, standing alone on the rocks has warned sailors away from the reef for almost two hundred years.

segments.label: B
segments.text: alone on the rocks has warned

questions.explanation: The parenthetical clause 'standing alone on the rocks' opens with a comma but is never closed. Segment B is missing the second comma, which belongs after 'rocks'.
